open-question.question: When a `tasks` call fails (the tool refusing, or git unavailable) for `ask-in-milestone-context`, `submit-task`, or `discuss-new-task`, do those three readers stop on a fixed line of their own, as `finish-current-milestone` and `derive-tasks` do, or proceed without the completed-task record?
open-question.recommendation: The stop belongs where a partial record leaves a lasting effect: submit-task writes and commits, so a failed read could land a duplicate of a completed task and it stops on one line in its existing family; ask-in-milestone-context and discuss-new-task change nothing, already rank the live deliverable first, and can still answer what the record never bore on, so they state the gap with the Error line and proceed, keeping the conversational skills' exemption from fixed lines.
open-question.alternative: `submit-task`, the one of the three that writes and commits, stops on a new fixed line of its own in its `Task not submitted — …` family, with the `Error:` line quoted verbatim below it and the line added to the `## Fixed console lines` table and its test, because its duplicate check against completed work would otherwise be incomplete. `ask-in-milestone-context` and `discuss-new-task` proceed without the completed-task record: each tells the user in prose that the completed-task read failed, quoting the `Error:` line, and carries on from its other reads (`requirements.md`, `TASKS_TODO.md`, the live deliverables), printing no fixed line. The stop falls exactly where a partial record can cause a lasting effect, a duplicate task committed into `TASKS_TODO.md`, while the read-only and talk-only skills still answer what they can and say what they could not see, and the conversational skills keep their exemption from fixed lines. The five readers no longer share one failure rule: two of them answer on a known-partial record, so a question about how a task turned out gets an answer grounded only in live deliverables (and, with git absent, no commit lens either), relying on the user to weigh the stated gap.

All three readers treat a failed `tasks` call (the tool refusing, or git unavailable) as a stop, exactly as the recorded decision has `finish-current-milestone` and `derive-tasks` do: each stops on a fixed line of its own, with the tool's one `Error:` line quoted verbatim below it, writing, committing, answering, and discussing nothing. `submit-task` gains a stop line in its existing `Task not submitted — …` family (such as `Task not submitted — the completed-task read failed.`), and `ask-in-milestone-context` and `discuss-new-task` each gain their first fixed line. All three lines join the `## Fixed console lines` table and its test, and the table's sentence naming `discuss-new-task` and `ask-in-milestone-context` among the purely conversational skills that print no fixed line of their own is revised. One failure rule at all five sites the readers' `tasks` calls decision set up as one fixed call shape, so every reader of the completed-task record behaves alike and a headless harness can tell which stop ended any of them; no reader ever answers or triages on a silently partial record. It ends the two conversational skills' exemption from fixed lines, a plugin-wide convention the table states, for a condition that rarely stands alone (an absent git also fails `submit-task`'s commit, and a refused path means a milestone directory found neither in the tree nor in history, where the other reads fail too), and it refuses an answer to questions such as "what's left?" that never needed the completed-task record.

All three readers stop on a failed `tasks` call, but only `submit-task` stops on a new fixed line of its own in its `Task not submitted — …` family, with the `Error:` line quoted verbatim below it and the line added to the `## Fixed console lines` table and its test. `ask-in-milestone-context` and `discuss-new-task` stop in prose: they tell the user the completed-task read failed, quote the `Error:` line, and neither answer nor discuss, printing no fixed line, so they stay outside the table as purely conversational skills. Every reader refuses to work on a partial record, matching `finish-current-milestone` and `derive-tasks` in behaviour, while the only skill a headless chain runs and matches by its first line, `submit-task`, gets the one new listed line, and the conversational skills' no-fixed-line convention stands. The conversational skills still refuse questions and discussions that need no completed-task record, and their stop, worded freely, gives a harness nothing to match if one ever drives them; two kinds of stop (listed and prose) now answer one condition.

None of the three stops. Each proceeds without the completed-task record and says so, quoting the tool's `Error:` line: `ask-in-milestone-context` and `discuss-new-task` tell the user in prose and carry on from their other reads, and `submit-task` runs its triage against `TASKS_TODO.md` and `requirements.md` only, ending its run on whichever line it would otherwise print, with the `Error:` line below that first line, its success report revised from exactly one line to allow it. No new fixed console line is added. No reader is ever blocked by a failure that, for these three, rarely stands alone (an absent git already fails `submit-task`'s commit with the commit tool's own `Error:`, and a refused path means a milestone directory whose other files are missing too), and no fixed line or table row is added for a condition practically always reported elsewhere. `submit-task` can commit a duplicate of a completed task when the read fails on its own, and in a headless chain its success line still matches as a clean end, the gap visible only in a line below it that a harness matching first lines does not read; the readers differ from `finish-current-milestone` and `derive-tasks`, which stop on the same failure.

The three readers' files state nothing about a failed `tasks` call: each shows its unconditional `tasks` call as the readers' `tasks` calls decision fixes it, and on a failure the runner acts by its own judgment, as these skills already do for any other failed read. No fixed line, prose instruction, or table row is added; a rule can be added later if a field run meets the case. The smallest change: it adds no text or line for a condition that, for these three, practically never arises on its own (git is the workflow's bootstrap prerequisite, and a refused path is a milestone directory found neither in the tree nor in history), so the milestone's edit to these readers stays the call swap alone. Behaviour on the failure is unpinned and untestable, may differ per run and per host, and can include `submit-task` silently committing a duplicate or a conversational answer presented as complete; it leaves the one fixed call shape at five sites with a failure rule at only two of them.

open-question.question: Which date does a `tasks` line carry, the commit's author date or its committer date, and does the newest-first order follow that same date or git's default log order, given that the two dates differ once a commit is rebased or amended?
open-question.recommendation: Author date keeps the day the task was completed through a rebase or amend and matches the author-date convention the draft fixes for finish dates; sorting the already-read records by that timestamp makes newest first a plain property of the printed column, statable without a graph exception and pinnable by a test with crafted dates, for one sorted call over fields the tool reads anyway.
open-question.alternative: Each `tasks` line's date field is the commit's author date (`%ad`/`%at`), and the tool orders the lines newest first by that same author timestamp itself, sorting the path-scoped log's commits after it reads them, so the printed date column is monotone whatever the commit graph says; git's own traversal order is not relied on. The date stays the day the task was actually completed through any rebase or amend, which keeps the attribution the draft already relies on (its migration copies the original author date so "the record's dates stay the finish dates"), and the order can never contradict the printed date, so a reader or a test can pin "newest first" as a plain property of the column. The tool carries a sort step and a second timestamp read of its own where git could order for it, and after a rebase that reorders commits a task can be listed below one that the history shows came before it, so the print's order and the graph's order disagree; the case is untested in practice, since none of the 174 recorded `Task-completion:` commits differs between its two dates by even a day.

Each line's date field is the commit's author date, and the order is the one git produces with `--author-date-order`: newest first by author timestamp, except that git never shows a parent before all its children, so where a rebase has given a child an older author date than its parent the graph wins; the tool adds no sort of its own. Keeps the author date's stable "when the task was done" meaning while letting git do the ordering in the one log call, so the order follows the printed date everywhere the history allows and the tool holds no sorting code. Newest first holds only up to the graph constraint, so a rebased or reordered branch can print a date column that is out of order, and the contract has to state that exception rather than a plain monotone order; it also ties the line shape to a git option whose interplay with path limiting and merges a test must pin on the shared fixtures.

Each line's date field is the commit's author date, and the order is git's default log order, which walks history newest first by committer timestamp (children before parents); the tool passes no ordering option and sorts nothing. The simplest call, with no ordering flag and no sort code, carrying the stable completion date the draft's history-side design assumes; on this repository's log the two dates never differ by a day and both orders are already monotone, so the print looks identical to the sorted forms in every recorded case. Order and printed date follow two different clocks, so once a commit is rebased or amended (its committer date moving, its author date not) the date column can visibly run out of order with no rule the contract can state beyond "git's order", which is exactly the divergence the question names and a later reader might take for a defect.

Each line's date field is the commit's committer date (`%cd`/`%ct`), and the order is git's default log order, which is newest first by that same committer timestamp; the tool passes no ordering option and sorts nothing, so the date printed and the date ordered by are one clock. Order and printed date agree by construction with no flag and no sort code, so newest first holds for the column in every history without clock skew, and the date is the moment the commit reached the history the reader is looking at. A rebase, amend, or cherry-pick moves the date to the day the commit was rewritten, so a task can show a date it was not completed on, and the field departs from the author-date convention the draft's migration and later history-side queries assume for finish dates, leaving the tool family with two date meanings unless a later milestone changes one; under clock skew the default order can still print a non-monotone column.

open-question.question: Is the fixed line that the inline `complete-task` skill's call and the `complete-task` agent's call print when their non-blank test refuses an empty acceptance bar a listed entry of the `## Fixed console lines` table, one line printed by both calls, or an in-call message like the orchestrator's `path file empty`, outside the table, given that the runner fixes the bar and runs the call again rather than ending the run?
open-question.recommendation: The line is a mid-run retry prompt for the runner and never a report's first line, so it stays outside the table like path file empty and dirty before start; but the empty-bar refusal moves out of a tested tool into shell prose, and an empty-bar case in the two call tests this milestone already rewrites keeps the guard pinned by behaviour, proving the call removes no section and writes or commits nothing.
open-question.alternative: The line is an in-call message outside the table, one shared identifier-free text printed by both calls, as in the unpinned option, but the fixed-call tests that already extract and run the two calls (`test_completion_call_lock_retry.py` for the inline skill's call, `test_parallel_completion.py` for the agent's step-5 call) each gain an empty-bar case asserting that the call prints exactly that line, removes no section, and writes or commits nothing. The table, its preamble, and its test stay unchanged. The guard is checked by behaviour, not just by the presence of a string: the test proves that an empty bar stops the call before `remove` and before any commit or path-file write, which is the property the guarding decision exists for, the way `test_sweep_batched_call.py` pins `dirty before start`, and the table keeps its first-line-only rule. It adds an empty-bar case to two call tests that this milestone already rewrites for `remove` and the body, making those tests larger, and the line is still not checked against every host tree's prose the way a table row is, so a wording change made in prose alone would not be caught.

The non-blank test's line is an in-call message outside the `## Fixed console lines` table: one short identifier-free text (in the style of `path file empty`) printed by both the inline `complete-task` skill's call and the agent's step-5 call, which the runner reads beside the call's other output and answers by fixing the bar and running the call again. It never opens a report, the table and its preamble stay unchanged, and no test checks the line beyond the call text the fixed-call tests already extract, exactly as the orchestrator's `path file absent` / `path file empty` lines (and the new `body file absent` / `body file empty`) stand today. It matches the existing precedent for every message a fixed call prints for its own runner to act on (`path file empty`, `dirty before start`, `stopped at`, the landed markers), keeps the table's rule that it lists only lines that end a run plus the one verdict, and costs no test, row, or new kind. Nothing pins the line: the two calls can drift apart, or the test can lose its message, with no test failing, since unlike the sweep's `dirty before start` no test runs a completion call on an empty bar; and if the agent's test ends up checking a body file rather than a held value (the "Agent bar holding form" question), one shared text may describe one call's test less accurately than the other's.

The line is listed in the `## Fixed console lines` table as one row naming both sources, the inline `complete-task` skill and the `complete-task` agent, the way the shared `Answer recorded.` row names three skills, so both calls print one identical text. Because it is printed mid-run and the runner fixes the bar and runs again rather than ending, it gets a new kind beside success, no-op, stop, and verdict (a retry line), and the table's preamble gains a sentence for it as it gained one for the verdict line. `test_fixed_console_lines.py` then checks it verbatim in every host tree and keeps it unique. The existing table test pins the text in every rendered tree with no new test code, so the two calls cannot drift apart without a row changing, and a harness reading a transcript gets one listed string for the empty-bar retry. It breaks the table's stated scope, which lists lines that open a report plus one verdict: a line no final message ever opens with needs a new kind and a preamble exception, and it sets a precedent that would also pull `path file empty`, `body file empty`, `dirty before start`, and the landed markers into the table; and one shared text only works if both calls test the same thing (a condition set by the "Agent bar holding form" question).

The line is listed in the table as two rows, one for the inline `complete-task` skill's call and one for the agent's step-5 call, each with its own text, distinct because the table's test refuses a repeated line, under the same new retry kind and preamble sentence the shared-row option needs. Each text names what its own call tests, for example a held value in the inline call and a held value or body file in the agent's call. Each row is pinned in every host tree by the existing table test, and each call's line can describe its own test exactly, so it stays accurate however the agent ends up holding the bar, with no assumption that the two tests are identical. It carries every cost of listing (a new kind, a preamble exception, a precedent for the other in-call lines) and adds a second listed line for what is one condition, the empty bar, which goes against the convention that a condition shared by several runners has one line; the distinction pays off only if the agent's test differs from the inline one (the "Agent bar holding form" question).
